analytic.title: Capacity-based Admission Control for Mixed Periodic and Aperiodic Real Time Service Processes

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents an on-line admission control algorithm for one-time aperiodic service requests and periodically generated service processes with real time constraints. Both types of service requests dynamically come and leave the system at run time, making any off-line analysis infeasible. During admission test, periodic task schedulability is determined by using per-task fixed capacity policy to account for the rate of each task. Aperiodic requests are admitted using any remaining capacity after periodic tasks. At run time, earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling is used to reduce context switch overhead. The proposed admission control is simpler than the traditional EDF analysis for mixed workload of periodic and aperiodic service processes. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm achieves 10-40% gain in system utilization compared with earlier fixed-priority, bound-based admission test, while incurs only sub-millisecond overhead for each service request.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: As Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and delivery model such as SaaS develops, more software is accessed via Internet, in the form of composable service components. Such service components are usually independently developed and can be integrated to execute on some common platform, such as the Compute Unit abstraction of Amazon EC2. Many applications are composed of distributed service components that have tight interactions and end-to-end real time requirements. Examples include real time enterprise, industrial process control, scientific workflow, and shared sensor network [1] [2]. In many applications, user-initiated aperiodic real time requests are mixed with periodic workflows such as real time sensor data processing in a system. This creates unique technical challenges due to the mixed workload and dynamic nature of service requests.

This paper presents an on-line admission control algorithm to meet the real time requirements of mixed periodic and aperiodic service processes in a dynamic SOA environment. Previous literature on aperiodic scheduling such as constant bandwidth server (CBS) [3] offers an approach to handle both periodic and aperiodic tasks. But it is designed for independent tasks rather than processes with precedence constraints that are prolific in service oriented applications. Offset-based schedulability analysis [4] can be applied to distributed real time systems, but is NPcomplete and too complex to be used as on-line admission test. Authors in [5] derived the first aperiodic utilization bound (AUB) for both stand-alone and pipelined aperiodic tasks. Although their work can also incorporate periodic tasks, the bound is pessimistic in nature.

In this paper we propose the capacity-based admission (CBA) test algorithm for systems with both aperiodic and periodic real time service processes. The work is part of the RT-Llama [6] project which builds the middleware support for real time applications running on SOA. The main characteristics of our proposed algorithm include the following:

• It provides an on-line polynomial-time admission test for both aperiodic and periodic tasks. • It is designed for precedence-constrained distributed service processes. • It is implemented on the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling at runtime, with an achievable system utilization of the full system capacity.

We have designed the algorithm and implemented it for simulation study. Simulation results show that the algorithm can achieve in general 10-40% gain in system utilization compared with AUB and only incurs small (sub-millisecond) overheads, making it suitable for on-line admission test. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II describes aperiodic and periodic task model. Sec. III details the CBA algorithm. The performance of CBA is compared with AUB and hTBTree in Sec. IV. Sec. V discusses the related work and the paper concludes with Sec. VI.

div.head: A. Process Model
div.p: A real-time service process consists of a flow of component services executing on different host machines. Process SP i is characterized by 1) the initial release time r i ; 2) the end-to-end deadline D e2e i relative to r i ; 3) the period T i (Aperiodic service process can be thought as having T i = ∞); 4) a set of linked component services in the service flow {S i,j }, where j indicates the execution order of the services in the process i. For example, if SP i has three sequential component services, then they will be denoted as S i,1 , S i,2 and S i,3 according to the execution order. Each S i,j is assumed to have a known computation time of C i,j . The problem of admission test is to determine whether SP i can finish all its services' executions by the end-to-end deadline r i + D e2e i . According to the proportional deadline assignment described in [7], in a sequential service process SP i , service S i,j 's initial release time r i,j , intermediate deadline D i,j , and period T i,j can be assigned as follows:

div.p: After deriving per-service timing parameters, the admission test can be performed on each service independently on its respective host. A process is admitted if all component services are admitted. In the case when the admission test for any component service fails, either the intermediate deadline should be re-assigned or the service process must be re-composed [8]. In this paper we will focus on the admission of services to be executed on a single host machine.

Therefore, the computation time of P i is denoted as C i , the initial release time as r i , the relative deadline as D i , and the period as T i . To reduce task switching overheads, all periodic and aperiodic tasks are scheduled together using EDF at runtime. Due to the optimality of EDF in single-processor preemptive scheduling, any feasible non-EDF schedule can be transformed into an EDF schedule and still meet all deadlines [9]. Therefore, a system with only admitted jobs in any feasible schedule can be executed using EDF even if the admission test is not performed under EDF.

We have demonstrated that it is practical to emulate the EDF behavior on top of Sun's real time JVM and Solaris OS [6]. Since our goal is not to provide the exact server capacity at any time instant, during run time we will use EDF for both periodic tasks and aperiodic jobs scheduling. The EDF run time scheduling reduces context switch overheads and greatly simplifies the implementation.

At run time, jobs that have been released are kept in an EDF queue. The system also keeps a future queue, for those jobs that have been admitted but need to wait for their predecessor jobs to finish. The future queue must be taken into consideration when admitting a new real-time process, which is the main difference between the admission control reported in this paper and previous work.

div.head: III. CAPACITY-BASED ADMISSION CONTROL ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section, we first present the CBA admission control algorithm to admit aperiodic jobs and then include periodic tasks.

div.head: A. Admission of Aperiodic Jobs
div.p: In CBA, aperiodic jobs are prioritized according to their absolute deadlines. A job ready to execute can preempt any executing job with a lower priority. Together all aperiodic jobs compete for the service time provided by the aperiodic server A. For a given aperiodic job J i , the computation demand in its job interval [r i , r i + D i ], denoted h(J i ), is the sum of:

• the remaining computation of higher-priority aperiodic jobs at time instant r i ; • the computation of higher-priority aperiodic jobs with arrival time r ≥ r i and absolute deadline d < r i +D i ; • J i 's own computation requirement C i . To admit an aperiodic job J, we must ensure 1) J itself can meet its deadline; 2) all jobs that are already admitted and have a lower priority (later deadline) than J can still meet their deadlines. Note that admitting a new job may affect the schedulability of a lower priority job whose job interval is totally disjoint with that of the new job. For example, consider a system with two admitted jobs J 1 (r = 5, d = 15, C = 6) and J 2 (10,16,4). If we want to admit a new job J(0, 10, 7), we have to re-admit both J 1 and J 2 , even though J 2 's job interval is disjoint with J's. In this example, J 2 would miss its deadline if J is admitted. Therefore, we must check every lower priority job of J if J is to be admitted. Algorithm 2 is the algorithm for checking if J can be admitted. It works by checking the computation demand (Lines 15-17) for the new job J to be admitted and all lower priority jobs that are already admitted. Line 4-6 calculate aperiodic computation from higher jobs at the J's release time. Lines 7-12 build J's OO list and add up computation from J's OO jobs. If J can meet its deadline, it is tentatively admitted (Line 19) and J.RC, J.AC are updated on each OO job's release time (Lines 21-24). Then, the algorithm recursively re-admits J's successor. If any of the existing jobs cannot meet its deadline in the process, J is rejected and the changes made to the existing jobs are rolled back.

Since the algorithm is recursive on each lower priority job of J, the overall time complexity is O(n 2 (lg n + m)).

div.head: IV. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: This section compares the proposed CBA admission control with two other on-line admission control methods: AUB [5] and hTBTree [10]. To verify the correctness of the proposed algorithm, we implemented an EDF simulator that schedules all admitted jobs to see if any deadline is missed. We have implemented the idle resetting mechanism in AUB to reduce the pessimism in AUB. Among all jobs admitted by CBA, no deadline miss is observed.

We simulate a pipelined process invoking services in sequence on N hosts. Service computation time on each host is randomly generated and independent of each other. The target task model for AUB is the "liquid" task model [5], where the task ratios (ratio of computation time to relative deadline) are very small, ranging from 0.01 to 0.1. In addition to that, we also consider "bulk" tasks with relative larger task ratios ranging from 0.1 to 0.3. The end-to-end relative deadline is calculated by dividing the sum of service computation time by the task ratio. In our simulation, Dmax Dmin ≈ 50. For CBA and hTBTree, we use proportional deadline assignment to assign per-service intermediate deadlines from end-to-end deadline.

Fig. 4-7 show the average system utilization with only aperiodic workload. To explore whether the pipeline length and the generated intermediate deadlines will impact the system utilization, admission tests for both single-service and 6-service processes are conducted. System utilization for liquid aperiodic workload (no periodic workload, # of hosts = 1). System utilization for bulk aperiodic workload (no periodic workload, # of hosts = 1). Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 show the single service scenario for both liquid and bulk tasks. From Fig. 4 we can see CBA and hTBTree can achieve almost full system utilization for liquid tasks. Since AUB uses fixed-priority scheduling, the utilization is about 10% lower. As offered traffic increases, all three curves converge to 100% utilization. For bulk tasks (Fig. 5), average system utlizations drops because it becomes harder to admit a job of bigger granularity. The margin between CBA and hTBTree is about 3-4 percent, while AUB degrades 10-20% in this case.

Fig. 67show the per-host average utilization for a process with 6 sequential services. Because of the "all or nothing" admission policy, one service rejection will result in the rejection of the entire process. Comparing Fig. 6 (Fig. 7) with Fig. 4 (Fig. 5), we can see the proportional deadline assignment only slightly affects the average system utilization. This is due to the workload is evenly distributed among the 6 hosts. For bulk tasks (Fig 7), CBA achieves a utilization gain of about 9 percent over hTBTree and 33 percent over AUB at the workload of 1.2.

Fig. 8-9 take periodic tasks into admission test and compare the per-host average utilizations (including periodic utilization if present) for a 6-service process. Because hTBTree is designed for only aperiodic jobs, it is not included in the experiment. If periodic tasks are present, the total capacity assigned to periodic tasks on each host is i Ci Di = 0.8, or about 15% periodic utilization. The goal of the experiemnt is to explore whether including periodic tasks will affect the effectiveness of the admission test. For liquid task model (Fig 8), CBA is able to admit enough small aperiodic jobs to fill the "gap" between active periodic jobs, resulting higher overall utilization when peiodic tasks are present. For bulk tasks (Fig 9 ), the acceptance ratio for CBA is lower compared to that of the liquid tasks, but the achievable overall utilization is still around 90%. With respect to AUB, we see some inconsistencies in overall utilization w/ and w/o periodic tasks for both liquid and bulk model. This is due to the fact that both types of workload share the same utilization bound, thus the inclusion of periodic tasks will reduce the effective aperiodic bound.

Fig 10 shows the average performance of invoking the admission tests for a single admission request on a PC with a 2.4GHz processor. Because of the need to ensure the schedulability of both the current job and all existing jobs (the O(n 2 ) part of the algorithm), CBA has the most runtime overhead. However, the sub-millisecond overhead still makes it feasible for on-line admission test. The hTBTree method has a very small overhead at a low workload, at the expense of a huge memory consumption. As workload increases to above 1.2, hTBTree needs to make more costly re-schedule operations to prevent unnecessary job rejections, making the performance comparable to that of CBA. Being a bound-based admission test, AUB has the lowest admission overhead, as expected.

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: Dynamic priority servers on EDF-based scheduling algorithms can handle both real time periodic and aperiodic tasks [11]. But the emphasis is to enhance the responsiveness of aperiodic tasks rather than to give them real Average admission overhead for a single request admission on one host. time guarantee. Constant Bandwidth Server [3] guarantees aperiodic tasks by assigning each task a bandwidth equal to its's computation time divided by its deadline. However, in a precedence-constrained process the bandwidth is overreserved because the relative deadline for each periodic task is less than the end-to-end deadline. CBA takes advantage of the unused capacity by exactly evaluating the aperiodic service time within each aperiodic job interval, thus avoid system under-utilization.

End-to-end schedulability analysis such as offsetbased analysis [4] [12] targets specifically at precedenceconstrained distributed systems. The basic idea is to compute the response time of periodic tasks under the worstcase arrival pattern, taking task offset into consideration. The worst-case response time on a predecessor host then determines the task offsets on the next host, etc. The original problem proves to be computationally intractable and pseudo-polynomial approximation algorithm has been proposed. The complexity of this approach prevents its usage as an on-line admission test. Meta-schedulability test [13] performs reduction-based end-to-end analysis and has the advantage of achieving consistent system utilization independent of process size. However, it still needs to rely on single-processor utilization bound such as AUB.

AUB proposes the first aperiodic utilization bound [14] to handle aperiodic jobs. It is extended for pipelined process structure in [5]. Because it is based on utilizationbound, it incurs very low run time overhead. However, it only works well for liquid task model. Furthermore, in the presence of mixed workloads, part of the utilization bound need to be reserved for periodic tasks, making the available aperiodic utilization bound very pessimistic. In comparison, CBA uses capacity mechanisms to admit periodic and aperiodic tasks. Therefore the admission of aperiodic jobs can fully utilize any remaining capacity left by periodic tasks.

Exact admission control algorithms such as [15][16] are based on the concept of processor demand and pure EDF scheduling. Complexity is drastically increased when including periodic tasks [15]. Also, both algorithms are for stand alone tasks.

The hTBTree method was used in the RT-Llama project earlier to reserve aperiodic processes. It provides a quick capacity check using a tree-based data structure to represent the future capacity [10]. The drawback of hTBTree is its memory requirement depends on how far in advance an application needs to reserve and the application's real time granularity. In the case of a long advance reservation time and very fine time granularity, the memory requirement can be prohibitively large.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a polynomial-time on-line admission control algorithm for real time processes deployed using the service-oriented paradigm. During admission control, periodic and aperiodic tasks are associated with different capacity to determine the schedulability. At any time, the sum of the capacity of all periodic and aperiodic servers is equal to the system capacity. EDF is used at run time to schedule the admitted task set without distinguishing between task types, avoiding the excessive context switch overhead of providing the exact server capacity at any time instant. Compared with the available bound-based admission control, the proposed capacity-based admission generally achieves 10-40% gain in system utilization. The gain is more prominent for bulk task model, where the ratio of compution time to relative deadline is large (0.1-0.3). The small (sub-millisecond) overhead incurred during admission makes the algorithm well-suited for on-line usage.

For future work we want to extend the sequential process structure to more general DAG structures. Also, an admission test failure does not necessarily entail rejection of the complete process. Intermediate deadlines can be reassigned based on the available capacity returned by the admission test. This will be especially important when a process needs to run on hosts of imbalanced workloads.
